borders.before: the lecturer's welcome, personal introduction, and explicit lecture learning outcomes
borders.after: the core definition of cancer as a genetic, evolutionary disease with microenvironmental requirements
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 1 is opening framing, whereas subtopic 2 begins the substantive lecture material on cancer biology.
borders.caseForMoving: Moving is not sensible because subtopic 1 is strictly administrative and introductory framing.
borders.caseForRemoving: Removing would combine introductory framing with core subject content.

borders.before: broad epidemiological patterns and geographical variations in cancer incidence across populations
borders.after: specific carcinogenic mechanisms, starting with infectious pathogens such as bacteria, viruses, and parasites
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 6 concludes the macro-level overview and epidemiology, while subtopic 7 starts the systematic walkthrough of specific classes of carcinogenic agents.
borders.caseForMoving: Subtopic 6 is still discussing global epidemiological maps, while subtopic 7 introduces pathogen mechanisms; subtopic 7 is the exact boundary.
borders.caseForRemoving: Joining would lump the broad conceptual/epidemiological framing with detailed molecular mechanisms of specific carcinogens.

borders.before: tissue-specific metabolic activation of carcinogens in cigarette smoke and industrial chemicals
borders.after: the role of non-mutagenic environmental agents (asbestos) acting via chronic inflammation and the initiator-promoter paradigm
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 14 shifts the focus from direct/metabolic mutagens to tumor promotion, inflammation, and host susceptibility.
borders.caseForMoving: Subtopic 13 is still about chemical carcinogen metabolism (beta-naphthylamine), whereas subtopic 14 explicitly pivots to agents that do not cause direct DNA damage (asbestos / promoters).
borders.caseForRemoving: Both cover carcinogenic mechanisms, but initiation vs promotion represents a major conceptual pivot.

borders.before: a summary of direct mutagens, promoters, and host developmental susceptibility factors
borders.after: methods for identifying and proving carcinogenicity using mutational signatures and genomic sequencing
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 17 provides a summary of biological/chemical mechanisms, and subtopic 18 starts discussing experimental and analytical methodologies.
borders.caseForMoving: Subtopic 17 is clearly a summary of the prior section on mechanisms and host factors.
borders.caseForRemoving: The causes/biology of cancer are distinct from the methodology of how scientists prove and detect carcinogenicity.

borders.before: toxicological in vitro screening methods (Ames test) and their limitations
borders.after: concluding risk-benefit framing, summary of lecture themes, and farewell
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 22 is the lecture's closing framing and final wrap-up.
borders.caseForMoving: Subtopic 21 contains detailed experimental methodology regarding the Ames test, so the closing strictly begins at 22.
borders.caseForRemoving: The closing wrap-up should remain distinct from the methodological details.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 2-3 address the theoretical roulette wheel and intrinsic vs extrinsic nature of cancer, whereas 4-6 dive into real-world environmental mutagen examples and geographic epidemiology.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopics 2 through 6 all build a continuous high-level foundation linking intrinsic mutations, bad luck, environmental factors, and epidemiology before getting into specific agent mechanisms.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 7-8 focus on biological/infectious carcinogens, whereas 9-13 shift to dietary toxins, radiation, and chemical xenobiotics.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: They all systematically cover specific classes of mutagens and direct DNA-damaging mechanisms.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 14-15 define the initiator vs promoter paradigm, while 16-17 explore host developmental age, tissue susceptibility, and summarize.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Both parts explore non-classical mutagenic factors—microenvironmental promotion, inflammation, and host cellular context—that modify cancer development.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 18-19 focus on human genomics and population biobanks, while 20-21 focus on animal bioassays and in vitro bacterial testing.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopics 18 through 21 form a unified review of the methodologies (sequencing, epidemiology, animal models, Ames test) used to prove carcinogenicity.

topics.label: Lecture Introduction and Learning Objectives
topics.groupedBecause: The lecturer introduces herself, outlines the scope of the cancer lecture course, and presents the core learning outcomes.

topics.label: Origins, Drivers, and Epidemiological Evidence of Cancer
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain cancer as an evolutionary genetic disease shaped by intrinsic biological errors, environmental exposures, and global epidemiological variations.

topics.label: Mechanisms of Pathogen, Chemical, and Physical Carcinogens
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics examine how infectious agents, dietary compounds, UV radiation, and metabolized chemical toxins induce specific types of DNA damage.

topics.label: Tumor Initiation, Promotion, and Host Susceptibility
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics discuss the non-mutagenic mechanisms of cancer promotion, chronic inflammation, and host developmental susceptibility.

topics.label: Methodologies for Assessing and Proving Carcinogenicity
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics detail the genomic, epidemiological, in vivo, and in vitro experimental approaches used to determine and validate carcinogenicity.

topics.label: Summary and Risk-Benefit Analysis
topics.groupedBecause: The lecturer wraps up the session with concluding remarks on balancing daily carcinogenic risks and benefits.
